result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give a clear size order with concrete point sizes, match Devanagari and Latin by apparent size and line height, choose one numeral system, and recommend embedding fonts plus a print test and a phone test. B is the only one that warns that a Latin font will hand Hindi off to a mismatched fallback and that an unembedded font silently turns into a default. It also adds a Hindi-reader proof check. A's separate phone layout and its tabular figures for the times are strong points, but A never covers the missing-glyph risk, so B edges ahead. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give concrete size ranks, sensible Devanagari/Latin pairing advice with extra size and leading for Hindi, consistent Western numerals with tabular figures, and proof-print and phone tests. A is more explicit that a Latin-only font won't render Hindi and will silently fall back. B adds more useful practical guidance: a separate phone layout, since A3 shrinks to about a fifth of its size on a phone, plus checking conjunct shaping, matching the names on the physical stop signs, and putting each stop's Hindi and English names in one row.
